opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a very natural development, and in many ways a healthy one. If you look at where the industry was a couple of years ago, there was a sense that the frontier would be held by a small number of closed labs, and everyone else would be following. What open-sourcing has done, especially from Chinese teams, is change that dynamic. When you release strong weights, the whole community can build on them, test them, find their weaknesses, and push them in directions you never anticipated. That feedback loop is extremely valuable.

For us, a few things matter. First, technical credibility. When you open-source a model, there's nowhere to hide. People will run it, benchmark it, and break it. If it holds up, that earns a kind of trust that marketing can't buy. Second, it's a way to attract talent and partners. The best researchers want to work on things that have real impact and visibility, and open models give them that. Third, it helps set standards. If your model becomes the base that many developers fine-tune or deploy, you're shaping how the ecosystem evolves.

Of course, people ask whether giving the model away undermines the business. I don't see it as a simple trade-off. The model weights are one part of the value. The real moat is the ability to keep producing the next, better model: the data, the infrastructure, the training know-how, and the speed of iteration. If you can keep moving fast, open-sourcing the current generation doesn't hurt you; it actually amplifies your influence. And for products, what users ultimately care about is the experience, how well the agent actually completes tasks, not just which weights sit underneath.

There's also a bigger-picture point. AI shouldn't be something that only a few companies control. Open models lower the barrier for researchers, startups, and developers around the world. I think Chinese companies have shown that you can be at or near the frontier and still be open, and that's pushed the whole field forward, including the closed labs.

So overall, I'm quite optimistic. The key is that open-sourcing isn't a substitute for doing the hard work on the technology itself. It only works if what you release is genuinely good. If it is, openness becomes a strong advantage rather than a cost.

r001.rationale: The response describes open-sourcing as changing industry dynamics, but does not identify market competition as a factor in Chinese companies’ decisions to open-source.

r002.rationale: It says the community can build on, test, and find weaknesses in released models, creating a valuable feedback loop that pushes the field forward, including toward the frontier.

fable-5.1.text:
I think open source is very important, and I think it's something I've thought a lot about.

If you look at the history of technology, open source has always been a very powerful force. It lowers the barrier for everyone, it accelerates the pace of iteration across the whole industry, and it allows the ecosystem to grow in ways that no single company could plan for. So from the perspective of the industry as a whole, I think more Chinese companies open-sourcing their models is a very positive thing. It means that developers in China, and actually developers around the world, can build on top of these models, and the collective progress becomes faster.

But I also want to be honest about the fact that open source is a means, not an end. The real question every company should ask is: what is your goal, and does open sourcing help you get there? For some companies, open source is a way to build an ecosystem, to attract talent, to establish a standard. For others, it's a way to catch up when you are behind, because when you are behind, you benefit more from the community than you lose by sharing. And for the companies at the very frontier, the calculation is different, because the gap between the frontier and the rest is exactly what creates value, and open sourcing the frontier model gives that away.

So I don't think there's one right answer. What I would say is that in the long run, I believe the most important thing is not open or closed, but whether you are actually pushing the frontier. If you are only open-sourcing something that is a copy of what already exists, that's useful, but it doesn't change the world. If you are open-sourcing genuinely new ideas, new architectures, new ways of doing things, then that's where the real contribution is. Open source is most powerful when it spreads innovation, not when it spreads imitation.

For us, we've released some of our work openly and kept other parts closed, and I think that's a reasonable way to balance it. We want to contribute to the community, especially on things like technical reports and ideas that help everyone, but we also need to make sure we have a sustainable path to keep doing frontier research. Ultimately, I think the companies that will be remembered are the ones that produced the ideas, regardless of whether they were open or closed.

r001.rationale: The response says open sourcing can help companies “catch up when you are behind” and contrasts that with frontier companies’ different incentives, identifying competitive position as a factor in the decision.

r002.rationale: The response says open sourcing helps developers build on models and makes collective progress faster, but it does not clearly connect learning across the community to progress toward the technological frontier.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a positive development. Open-sourcing models lowers the barrier for people to experiment, build applications, and contribute improvements. For Chinese companies, it’s also a way to reach developers globally. People can try the model directly and judge it by what it can do.

But I wouldn’t frame this purely as a choice between open and closed. The deeper question is whether a company can keep advancing the technology. Releasing a strong model is valuable; sustaining that level of research and investment is much harder. Companies need a business model that supports that cycle, whether through APIs, products, or services.

So I see open source as an important way to build an ecosystem. Ultimately, though, the impact depends on the quality of the models and whether people can use them to solve real problems.

r001.rationale: The response discusses reaching developers, business models, and sustaining research, but does not identify market competition as a reason for open-sourcing.

r002.rationale: It mentions contributing improvements and building an ecosystem, but does not say that learning from one another accelerates progress toward the technological frontier.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s a positive development. Open-sourcing models allows more developers to experiment, build applications, and contribute improvements. For Chinese companies, it’s also a way to reach developers globally: people can try the model directly and judge its capabilities for themselves.

Of course, releasing a model is only the beginning. The quality of the model, the tools around it, and continued support all matter. The interesting question is whether a company can turn that openness into a healthy ecosystem while building a sustainable business. I think open models and proprietary models will coexist, serving different needs.

r001.rationale: The response describes global reach and business sustainability, but does not identify market competition as a reason Chinese companies open-source models.

r002.rationale: It mentions developers contributing improvements, but does not say that learning from one another accelerates the community toward the technological frontier.
